sense: so much a day or a month: pay, interest, exchange

evidence: Tac. Ann. 1.17: dēnīs in diem assibus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin has no noun for a rate: it puts the price in the ablative and the unit after in, dēnīs in diem assibus, at ten asses a day; for every year, in singulōs annōs (Cic. Att. 6.3.5).

evidence: Sall. Cat. 37.7: manuum mercēde inopiam tolerāre (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: interest at one per cent a month, twelve a year
terms.comment: The standard Roman rate of interest; a third of it was triēns, two thirds bēs (Cic. Att. 4.15.7). See interest, on money lent.

terms.gloss: the rate of exchange; the money-changer’s premium

phrases.latin: dēnīs in diem assibus animam et corpus aestimārī
phrases.english: (they complain) that body and soul are valued at ten asses a day

phrases.latin: Scaptius centēsimīs, renovātō in singulōs annōs faenore, contentus nōn fuit
phrases.english: Scaptius was not content with twelve per cent, with the interest added to the debt every year

sources: Lewis & Short: in · Lewis & Short: merces · Lewis & Short: centesimus · Lewis & Short: collybus
